levels.brief:
# FLOOR 1 - Hello, Adventurer

You are standing at the bottom of a very tall tower. At the top is a game.
Not a game someone made for you - one you wrote. Every floor you clear adds a
piece of it.

This floor is the smallest possible piece: making the machine say a thing.

## The shape of every C++ program

```
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    std::cout << "text goes here\n";
    return 0;
}
```

Four things are happening.

- `#include <iostream>` pulls in the toolbox for input and output. Without it, `std::cout` does not exist.
- `int main()` is where your program starts. Every C++ program has exactly one.
- `std::cout << "..."` sends text to the screen. Read `<<` as an arrow pointing where the text goes.
- `return 0;` tells the operating system "I finished, nothing went wrong."

That `\n` is not two characters when it prints. Inside quotes it means **newline** - move to the next line. This is how you control layout.

## Chaining

`<<` can be chained, and this is very normal C++:

```
std::cout << "gold: " << 42 << "\n";
```

That prints `gold: 42` and then a newline. Notice the number has no quotes -
quotes mean "literal text", no quotes means "the value".

## Your task

Open your `main.cpp` and make the program print exactly these four lines:

```
==================================
  DUNGEON OF THE NULL POINTER
==================================
a game you have not written yet
```

Line up the spacing exactly. The trials compare character for character,
which is the first hard habit of programming: the computer does not do
what you meant.

## When you are ready

```
.\play.ps1 run      <- see it with your own eyes
.\play.ps1 check    <- face the trial
```

levels.brief:
# FLOOR 2 - The Character Sheet

Printing fixed text is a party trick. A game needs numbers that change:
health that drops, gold that grows. That means **variables**.

## A variable is a labelled box

```
int gold = 25;
```

Three parts: the **type** (`int`), the **name** (`gold`), the **starting
value** (`25`). From then on, the word `gold` means whatever is in the box.

```
gold = gold + 17;      // read the box, add 17, put it back
gold += 17;            // exactly the same thing, written shorter
```

## The types you need today

- `int` - whole numbers. Health, gold, damage. `int health = 100;`
- `double` - numbers with a fractional part. `double crit = 0.15;`
- `char` - exactly one character, in SINGLE quotes. `char rank = 'R';`
- `bool` - true or false, nothing else. `bool alive = true;`
- `std::string` - text. Needs `#include <string>` at the top. `std::string name = "Kaelen";`

## Two things that will bite you

**Bools print as numbers.** `std::cout << alive;` prints `1`, not `true`.
A bool really is 1 or 0 underneath. Later you will learn to print it nicely.

**Integer division throws away the remainder.** `7 / 2` is `3`, not `3.5`,
because both sides are ints. If you want `3.5` you need a `double` involved.
This one catches everybody, usually at 2am.

## Your task

Build a character sheet out of variables, not out of hardcoded text.
These are the **starting** facts:

- the hero is named `Kaelen`, and their class letter is `R`
- health starts at `120`, then a trap takes `20` off it
- gold starts at `25`, then they find `17` more
- strength is `5`, and attack damage is `strength * 2 + 3`
- crit chance is `0.15`
- the hero is alive

Print exactly this:

```
-- CHARACTER SHEET --
name: Kaelen
class: R
health: 100
gold: 42
attack: 13
crit: 0.15
alive: 1
```

> The trial checks your source too: the numbers `100`, `42` and `13` must not
> appear anywhere in your code. You have to make the program work them out.
> That is the whole point - a game where the health is typed in by hand is not
> a game.

levels.brief:
# FLOOR 3 - Naming the Hero

A game nobody can talk to is a screensaver. Time to read input.

## Two ways in

`std::cin` is the mirror image of `std::cout`. The arrows flip around,
because now data is flowing *out of* the input and *into* your variable:

```
int level;
std::cin >> level;          // read one number
```

`>>` stops at the first space. That is fine for numbers, and useless for
names, because `Grim the Unwashed` would only give you `Grim`. For a whole
line, use `getline`:

```
std::string name;
std::getline(std::cin, name);   // reads everything up to the Enter key
```

## Prompting

The player cannot read your mind, so print a prompt first:

```
std::cout << "What shall we call you?\n";
std::getline(std::cin, name);
```

That is the entire loop of interactive software: print, read, respond.

## Your task

Ask two questions, read the answers, and print a small hero summary.

1. print `What shall we call you?` then read a whole line into a string
2. print `How many floors have you climbed?` then read an int
3. print a blank line
4. print `<name>, level <n>`
5. print `max health: <80 + n * 20>`
6. print `next level at: <n * 100> xp`

With the player typing `Kaelen` and then `7`, the whole run looks like:

```
What shall we call you?
How many floors have you climbed?

Kaelen, level 7
max health: 220
next level at: 700 xp
```

> The prompts and the answers look interleaved when you type them yourself -
> that is just your keyboard echoing. The trials feed input from a file, so
> only your program's own output is compared.

## Try it yourself first

```
.\play.ps1 run
```

Type an answer, press Enter. That is your program listening to you.

levels.tagline: the first boss - make the program choose
hints: `if (hp < 30) { ... } else if (hp < 70) { ... } else { ... }` - the FIRST matching branch wins and the rest are skipped. That is why order matters.
`==` compares, `=` assigns. `if (hp = 0)` compiles and ruins your day. Comparison is always the doubled one.
`&&` is and, `||` is or. `if (hp < 30 && potions > 0)` means both must be true.
You wrote the status chain already - do the action as a SECOND, separate if/else chain below it. Two questions, two chains.

levels.brief:
# FLOOR 4 - The Fork in the Road   [BOSS]

Everything so far ran top to bottom, the same way every time. A game has to
*decide*. This is the floor where your program grows a brain stem.

## if / else if / else

```
if (health < 30) {
    std::cout << "critical\n";
} else if (health < 70) {
    std::cout << "wounded\n";
} else {
    std::cout << "healthy\n";
}
```

Read it as a ladder. The first rung that is true runs, and **everything below
it is skipped**. So the order is the logic. If you check `health < 70` first,
a hero on 5 health is merely "wounded" and the critical branch can never fire.

## The comparisons

`<` `>` `<=` `>=` compare. `==` asks "are these equal", `!=` asks "are these
different".

`=` is assignment, `==` is comparison. Writing `if (hp = 0)` does not test
anything - it *sets* hp to 0 and then treats 0 as false. This bug is a rite
of passage. Now you know.

## Combining conditions

```
if (health < 30 && potions > 0)     // both must be true
if (hasKey || hasLockpick)          // either one will do
if (!alive)                         // not alive
```

A bool is already a question's answer, so `if (hasKey)` is complete on its
own - you never need `if (hasKey == true)`.

## Your task

Read three integers, in this order:

- `hp` - the hero's health
- `potions` - how many potions they carry
- `hasKey` - 1 if they hold the iron key, 0 if not

Then print **two** lines.

**Line one** is the status, decided by hp alone:

- below 30 -> `status: critical`
- below 70 -> `status: wounded`
- otherwise -> `status: healthy`

**Line two** is what happens next. Check these in exactly this order:

1. hp is 0 or less -> `You are dead. The dungeon keeps your gold.`
2. hp below 30 and at least one potion -> `You drink a potion. Health back to 100.`
3. hp below 30 and no potions -> `You crawl toward the stairs, bleeding.`
4. hero has the key -> `You unlock the iron door and descend.`
5. anything else -> `You search the room for a key.`

For the input `25 1 0`:

```
status: critical
You drink a potion. Health back to 100.
```

For the input `90 0 1`:

```
status: healthy
You unlock the iron door and descend.
```

> A dead hero on 0 hp is still "critical" - the status line does not care
> about the action line. Two independent questions about the same numbers.

levels.title: The Training Dojo
levels.tagline: make the machine repeat itself
hints: The shape is: something before the loop that the condition looks at, and something inside the loop that changes it. `while (level < 5) { ... }` needs `level` to grow inside, or it never stops.
Count the sessions with a variable you declare BEFORE the loop and `++` at the top of each pass. If you declare it inside, it is reborn every time.
The level-up is an `if` INSIDE the while loop, checked after adding xp: `if (xp >= 100) { xp -= 100; ++level; ... }`.
Subtract 100, do not reset to 0 - the leftover xp carries over. That is why the totals after a level-up are 20, then 10, then 0, then 20.
levels.brief:
# FLOOR 5 - The Training Dojo

You can print, store and decide. What you cannot do yet is *repeat*, and
almost everything in a game is repetition: frames, turns, enemies, rounds.

## while

```
int count = 0;
while (count < 3) {
    std::cout << "swing\n";
    ++count;
}
```

Read it as: "as long as this is true, run the block again". Three parts,
and all three have to be there:

1. something set up **before** the loop (`count = 0`)
2. a condition that will eventually become false (`count < 3`)
3. something **inside** that moves toward that (`++count`)

Forget number 3 and the loop runs forever. Your program will hang, the
trials will report it, and you will have written your first infinite loop -
also a rite of passage.

## The shorthands

```
++count;        // add one
xp += 30;       // add 30
xp -= 100;      // take 100 away
```

## Your task

A hero trains until they reach level 5.

Set up: `xp` starts at 0, `level` starts at 1, `session` starts at 0.

Then, while the level is below 5:

- one more session happens, and 30 xp is earned
- print `session <n>: +30 xp (total <xp>)`
- if xp has reached 100 or more, spend 100 of it to gain a level, and print
  `  ** level up ** now level <level> (xp <leftover>)` - note the two leading spaces

When the loop finally ends, print `training done: <sessions> sessions to reach level 5`.

The first few lines look like this:

```
session 1: +30 xp (total 30)
session 2: +30 xp (total 60)
session 3: +30 xp (total 90)
session 4: +30 xp (total 120)
  ** level up ** now level 2 (xp 20)
session 5: +30 xp (total 50)
```

> The leftover matters. At 120 xp you spend 100 and keep 20 - you do not
> throw it away. Getting that right is the difference between a loop that
> models something and a loop that just counts.

Your program has to work out how many sessions it took. Typing the answer in
is forbidden by the trial, and honestly, you do not know it yet either.

levels.tagline: for loops, and dice that lie the same way twice
hints: `for (int i = 1; i <= 10; ++i) { ... }` packs the three parts of a while loop onto one line: set up, test, step.
Declare `hits` and `total` BEFORE the for loop. Anything declared inside is destroyed at the closing brace.
Call `roll(6)` exactly once per pass and store it: `int r = roll(6);`. If you call it twice you get two different numbers and your log will not match your total.
`if (r >= 4) { ++hits; }` and `total += r;` both go inside the same loop body, after the roll.
levels.brief:
# FLOOR 6 - The Dice Tower

Games need luck. Computers cannot do luck, so they fake it - very well, and
completely predictably. Today you meet both halves of that.

## for

A `while` loop that counts always has the same three moving parts, so C++
gives you a way to put all three on one line:

```
for (int i = 1; i <= 10; ++i) {
    std::cout << i << "\n";
}
```

- `int i = 1` runs once, before anything
- `i <= 10` is checked before every pass
- `++i` runs after every pass

Use `for` when you know how many times. Use `while` when you are waiting for
something to happen. That is the whole rule.

`i` only exists inside the loop. Anything you want to survive - a total, a
counter - must be declared **above** the loop.

## Dice that repeat themselves

Your `main.cpp` already contains this, as a gift:

```
unsigned int rngState = 20260908u;

int roll(int sides) {
    rngState = rngState * 1103515245u + 12345u;
    return (int)((rngState >> 16) % (unsigned int)sides) + 1;
}
```

You will learn to write functions like that on floor 9. For now, just call
it: `roll(6)` gives you 1 to 6, `roll(20)` gives you 1 to 20.

It is not really random. It stirs one number (`rngState`) with arithmetic and
serves you a slice of the result. Same starting state, same sequence, every
single run. That sounds like a flaw and it is a gift: your game is replayable,
your bugs are reproducible, and the trials can check your dice.

`%` is the leftover after division - `17 % 5` is `2`. It is how you squeeze a
huge stirred number down into the range 0..sides-1. The `+ 1` shifts it to
1..sides, because dice do not have a zero.

## Your task

Roll a six-sided die ten times. For each roll, print:

```
roll <n>: <value>
```

Count how many rolls were **4 or higher** (a hit), and add every roll into a
running total. When the loop is done, print:

```
hits: <h> of 10
damage: <total>
```

Because the dice are seeded, everyone's answer is the same one. Roll it
once per pass - `roll()` changes the state every time you call it, so
calling it twice in one pass gives you two different numbers and a log
that disagrees with your own total.

levels.brief:
# FLOOR 7 - The Combat Round

Loops, conditions and dice, in one room. This is a real combat system -
small, but the same shape as one in a real game.

## Loops that end when something happens

Not every loop counts. Some wait for a state to change:

```
while (heroHp > 0 && goblinHp > 0) {
    // one round
}
```

The loop stops the moment either fighter drops. But there is a subtlety:
the condition is only checked **between** rounds. If the hero kills the
goblin halfway through a round, the goblin still gets its swing, because the
code below has not run out yet.

`break` is the fix. It leaves the loop immediately, from anywhere inside:

```
if (goblinHp <= 0) {
    break;
}
```

Order of operations inside a turn is a design decision, and it is the kind
of thing that decides whether a fight feels fair.

## Your task

A hero (30 hp) fights a goblin (22 hp). Rounds repeat while both live.

Each round, in this order:

1. count the round
2. print `-- round <n> --`
3. the hero swings for `roll(6) + 2`, print `you hit the goblin for <d> (goblin hp <left>)`
4. if the goblin is at 0 or below, `break` out - a dead goblin does not swing
5. the goblin swings for `roll(4) + 1`, print `the goblin hits you for <d> (your hp <left>)`

When the fight is over, print one line:

- if the hero survived: `the goblin falls. you live, on <hp> hp.`
- otherwise: `you fall. the dungeon keeps your gold.`

The opening looks like this:

```
-- round 1 --
you hit the goblin for 6 (goblin hp 16)
the goblin hits you for 2 (your hp 28)
-- round 2 --
```

> The dice are the same seeded `roll()` from floor 6, so this fight plays out
> identically for everyone. If your log drifts from the expected one, count
> your `roll()` calls - an extra call anywhere shifts every number after it.

levels.tagline: the second boss - many things under one name
hints: `std::vector<std::string> pack;` starts empty. `pack.push_back(item);` adds one to the end. `pack.size()` says how many.
Read with `while (std::getline(std::cin, line))` and `if (line == "done") break;` inside. getline gives you the whole line, spaces and all.
To print numbered items you need the index, so use a counting loop: `for (size_t i = 0; i < pack.size(); ++i)` and print `i + 1` as the human number.
To search, walk the vector with a range-for and set a bool: `for (const std::string& item : pack) { if (item == "torch") hasTorch = true; }`

levels.brief:
# FLOOR 8 - The Inventory Rack   [BOSS]

One variable holds one thing. A backpack holds however many things the
player shoves into it, and you do not know that number when you write the
code. You need a container.

## std::vector

```
#include <vector>
#include <string>

std::vector<std::string> pack;    // empty, holds strings
pack.push_back("torch");          // now it holds one
pack.push_back("rope");           // now two
```

The `<std::string>` part says what kind of thing goes in. A
`std::vector<int>` holds ints. It grows by itself - that is the whole point.

```
pack.size()     // how many are in there
pack[0]         // the FIRST one. Counting starts at zero.
pack.back()     // the last one
pack.empty()    // true if there is nothing in it
```

**Zero-based indexing** is the thing to burn in. A vector with 4 items has
valid slots 0, 1, 2 and 3. There is no slot 4. Reaching for one is not an
error message - it is your program quietly reading someone else's memory,
and it is the single most common way C++ programs go wrong.

## Two ways to walk it

When you need the position:

```
for (size_t i = 0; i < pack.size(); ++i) {
    std::cout << i + 1 << ". " << pack[i] << "\n";
}
```

When you only need the things:

```
for (const std::string& item : pack) {
    std::cout << item << "\n";
}
```

The second is a **range-for**. Read it as "for each item in pack". The `&`
means "look at the real one, do not make a copy" - you will meet that
properly on floor 10.

## Your task

Read item names, one per line, until the line `done` arrives. Do not store
`done` itself. Then print the pack.

If nothing was picked up, print exactly one line and stop:

```
your pack is empty
```

Otherwise print:

```
-- PACK (<n> items) --
  1. <first>
  2. <second>
  ...
slots used: <n> of 8
torch: <yes or no>
last picked up: <the final item>
```

Each numbered line starts with two spaces. Items are numbered from 1 for
the human, even though the vector counts from 0 - translating between those
two is your job now.

`torch:` is `yes` only if an item is exactly `torch`.

With input `torch`, `rope`, `rations`, `iron key`, `done`:

```
-- PACK (4 items) --
  1. torch
  2. rope
  3. rations
  4. iron key
slots used: 4 of 8
torch: yes
last picked up: iron key
```

# FLOOR 9 - Spells as Functions

You have been calling `roll()` for three floors without knowing how it works.
Today you build your own.

A function is a piece of work with a name, an entrance and an exit. That is
all it is - and it is the single biggest jump in how large a program you can
hold in your head.

## The shape

```
int attackDamage(int strength) {
    return roll(6) + strength / 2;
}
```

- `int` at the front - what it hands **back**
- `attackDamage` - what you call it
- `(int strength)` - what you must hand **in**
- `return` - the value that comes out, and the instant exit

Call it like any value you have used:

```
int d = attackDamage(6);
```

## void

Some work produces no answer, only an effect - printing, for instance.
Those return `void`, and you just let them end:

```
void shout(const std::string& text) {
    std::cout << text << "!\n";
}
```

## Two rules that will trip you

**Define before you call.** C++ reads your file top to bottom. A function
must appear above whatever calls it - so your functions go between `roll()`
and `main()`.

**Parameters are local copies.** `strength` inside the function is not the
same box as the `strength` outside it. Changing it changes nothing out
there. That is not a limitation, it is a safety rail - and floor 10 is about
the door in that rail.

## Your task

Write exactly three functions, then use them.

```
int attackDamage(int strength)
```
returns `roll(6) + strength / 2`. (`strength / 2` is integer division - a
strength of 7 adds 3, not 3.5.)

```
bool isDead(int hp)
```
returns true when hp is 0 or below.

```
void showBar(const std::string& name, int hp, int maxHp)
```
prints one line: the name, a ten-cell bar, and the numbers.

```
ogre [######....] 18/30
```

The bar has exactly ten cells. Filled cells are `#`, empty ones are `.`,
and the count is `hp * 10 / maxHp` - except that a dead thing shows zero
filled cells rather than a negative number.

## Then, in main

The hero has strength 6. The ogre has 30 hp out of 30.

1. print `-- the ogre blocks the stair --`
2. `showBar` the ogre
3. for three rounds, numbered 1 to 3:
   - work out the damage with `attackDamage(6)`
   - take it off the ogre
   - print `round <n>: you deal <d>`
   - `showBar` the ogre again
4. finally, print `the ogre is down` if `isDead` says so, otherwise
   `the ogre still stands`

The first lines come out like this:

```
-- the ogre blocks the stair --
ogre [##########] 30/30
round 1: you deal 7
ogre [#######...] 23/30
```

# FLOOR 10 - What the Potion Touches

Last floor ended on a warning: parameters are copies. Today that warning
becomes the whole lesson, because it is the bug every beginner writes.

## The bug

```
void heal(int hp, int amount) {
    hp += amount;             // changes the copy
}

int myHp = 20;
heal(myHp, 30);
std::cout << myHp;            // still 20
```

The function was handed a *photocopy* of `myHp`. It scribbled on the
photocopy and threw it away. Nothing you do to a by-value parameter is
visible outside.

## The fix: a reference

```
void heal(int& hp, int amount) {
    hp += amount;             // changes the caller's actual variable
}
```

One `&` and `hp` stops being a copy - it becomes another name for the very
box the caller passed in. Writing to it writes to theirs.

## const&, and why it is everywhere

References have a second use that has nothing to do with changing things.
Copying a big object - a long string, a vector of 500 monsters - costs real
time. A reference costs nothing, because nothing is copied.

```
void describe(const std::string& name)
```

`const` promises you will only look, never touch. So `const&` means "let me
see the real one, cheaply, and I swear not to break it". For anything bigger
than an int, this is the default you should reach for. You have been reading
it since floor 8 - now you know what it says.

## Your task

Write four functions and drive them from main.

```
void brokenHeal(int hp, int amount)      // by VALUE - deliberately useless
void heal(int& hp, int maxHp, int amount) // by reference, never above maxHp
void wound(int& hp, int amount)           // by reference, never below 0
bool tryBuy(int& gold, int price)         // spends only if affordable
```

`tryBuy` returns true and subtracts the price when there is enough gold.
When there is not, it returns false and leaves the gold alone.

In main, start with `hp = 20`, `maxHp = 60`, `gold = 30`, and print exactly
this sequence:

```
hp 20
brokenHeal 30 -> hp 20
heal 30 -> hp 50
heal 30 -> hp 60
wound 80 -> hp 0
gold 30
buy rope for 10 -> yes, gold 20
buy sword for 50 -> no, gold 20
```

Read those two `heal` lines. The second one asks for 30 more and only gets
10, because 60 is the ceiling. And `brokenHeal` sits there doing nothing at
all, which is the entire point of this floor.

# FLOOR 11 - The Monster Blueprint

A goblin is a name, an amount of health, and an attack value. Three
variables that belong together. Right now your only option is:

```
std::string goblinName = "goblin";
int goblinHp = 12;
int goblinAttack = 3;
```

Now add an ogre. Now add twelve more. Now pass one to a function - all
three pieces, every time, in the right order. The idea "a monster" exists
in your head but nowhere in your code, and that gap is where bugs live.

## struct

```
struct Monster {
    std::string name;
    int hp;
    int attack;
};
```

That is a new **type**, as real as `int`. It says: a Monster is these three
things, always, together. Note the semicolon after the closing brace. C++
wants it and will be unpleasant about it.

## Using one

```
Monster goblin{"goblin", 12, 3};    // in declaration order

goblin.hp -= 5;                     // the dot reaches inside
std::cout << goblin.name;
```

## Structs through functions

Everything you learned on floor 10 applies, and matters more, because a
struct is bigger than an int:

```
void describe(const Monster& m)     // only looking - cheap, and safe
void wound(Monster& m, int amount)  // changing the caller's monster
```

This is the moment your code starts describing the *game* instead of
describing memory.

## Your task

Declare the `Monster` struct exactly as above, then write three functions:

```
void describe(const Monster& m)
```
prints one line: `<name>  hp <hp>  atk <attack>` - two spaces before `hp`
and two before `atk`.

```
bool alive(const Monster& m)
```
true when the monster's hp is above 0.

```
void wound(Monster& m, int amount)
```
takes hp off, never below 0.

In main, make two monsters - `goblin` with 12 hp and 3 attack, and `ogre`
with 30 hp and 7 attack - and produce exactly this:

```
-- the room --
goblin  hp 12  atk 3
ogre  hp 30  atk 7
you swing at the goblin for 9
goblin  hp 3  atk 3
goblin alive: yes
you swing at the goblin for 9
goblin  hp 0  atk 3
goblin alive: no
the ogre turns to face you
ogre  hp 30  atk 7
```

Both swings do 9 damage. The second one takes the goblin from 3 to 0, not
to -6, because `wound` has a floor.

# FLOOR 12 - A Room Full of Monsters   [BOSS]

Floor 8 gave you a vector of strings. Floor 11 gave you a Monster. Put them
together and you have the thing every game is actually made of: a list of
entities you loop over, change, and ask questions about.

## A vector of structs

```
std::vector<Monster> room;
room.push_back(Monster{"goblin", 12, 3});
```

## The trap that will get you

```
for (Monster m : room) {      // m is a COPY
    wound(m, 5);              // the copy takes damage
}                             // the copy is destroyed. room is untouched.
```

```
for (Monster& m : room) {     // m is the real one
    wound(m, 5);              // the room actually changes
}
```

One character. This is floor 10's lesson in a different coat, and it is worth
meeting twice, because when it bites you in real code it looks like the
computer is ignoring you.

Use `const Monster&` when you are only reading, `Monster&` when you are
changing. Say what you mean and the compiler will hold you to it.

## Your task

Read monsters from input. Each is a name, an hp and an attack:

```
goblin 12 3
ogre 30 7
rat 4 1
done
```

The word `done` on its own ends the list. Names never contain spaces, so
`std::cin >>` is fine here.

`describe`, `alive` and `wound` from floor 11 are already in your starter
file. Use them.

Then print, in this order:

1. `-- ROOM (<n> monsters) --`
2. every monster, via `describe`
3. `total threat: <sum of every attack value>`
4. `toughest: <name of the monster with the most hp>` - on a tie, the first one
5. `-- you sweep the room --`
6. one swing at each monster, in order, for `roll(6) + 3` damage:
   - `you hit <name> for <d> (hp <left>)`
   - and if that killed it, a second line: two spaces, the name, ` dies`
7. `still standing: <how many are still alive>`

If the room is empty, print only this and stop:

```
-- ROOM (0 monsters) --
nothing here but dust
```

For the three monsters above, the sweep begins:

```
-- you sweep the room --
you hit goblin for 7 (hp 5)
you hit ogre for 6 (hp 24)
you hit rat for 7 (hp 0)
  rat dies
```

> One `roll(6)` per monster, in order. An extra call anywhere and every
> number after it shifts.

hints: `size_t space = line.find(' ');` gives you the position of the first space, or `std::string::npos` when there is none.
When there IS no space the whole line is the verb and the rest is empty. When there is one: `verb = line.substr(0, space);` and `rest = line.substr(space + 1);`
`substr(start)` runs to the end of the string. `substr(start, count)` takes count characters. Getting these two mixed up is most of what goes wrong with strings.
Order your checks: empty line first, then look, then go, then take, then the catch-all. And test the `rest.empty()` case inside go and take before using it.

levels.brief:
# FLOOR 13 - The Parser's Tongue

A player types `take rusty key`. Your game has to turn that sentence into a
verb, a thing, and an action. That is parsing, and it is the seam between a
human and a program.

## The string toolbox

```
std::string line = "take torch";

line.size()            // 10
line.empty()           // false
line.find(' ')         // 4  - position of the first space
line.substr(0, 4)      // "take"
line.substr(5)         // "torch"  - from 5 to the end
```

`substr(start, count)` takes `count` characters. `substr(start)` takes
everything from there on. Mixing those two up is most of what goes wrong
with strings.

## npos

What does `find` return when there is no space at all?

```
std::string::npos
```

A special "nowhere" value. You must check for it, because `substr` given a
nonsense position will throw:

```
size_t space = line.find(' ');
if (space == std::string::npos) {
    verb = line;          // the whole line is the verb
    rest = "";
} else {
    verb = line.substr(0, space);
    rest = line.substr(space + 1);
}
```

## The pitfall you were promised on floor 3

```
std::cin >> level;                  // reads 7, leaves the Enter key sitting there
std::getline(std::cin, name);       // grabs that leftover Enter. Empty string.
```

`>>` stops at whitespace and does not consume the newline. The next
`getline` finds it immediately and returns nothing. The cure:

```
std::cin >> level;
std::cin.ignore(10000, '\n');       // throw away the rest of that line
std::getline(std::cin, name);
```

Today you only use `getline`, so you dodge it. Now you know why the order
mattered back then, and what to do when it does not.

## Your task

Read lines until the line `quit` (or until the input runs out). For each
line, print exactly one response.

- an empty line -> `say something.`
- `look` -> `the room is dark.`
- `go <somewhere>` -> `you walk <somewhere>.`
- `take <thing>` -> `you pocket the <thing>.`
- `go` or `take` with nothing after it -> `<verb> what?`
- anything else -> `you cannot <verb>.`

The `<somewhere>` and `<thing>` are the whole rest of the line, spaces and
all - `go down the stairs` gives `you walk down the stairs.`

When the loop ends, print `you leave the room.` exactly once.

Input:

```
look
go north
take torch
dance
quit
```

Output:

```
the room is dark.
you walk north.
you pocket the torch.
you cannot dance.
you leave the room.
```

levels.tagline: data that knows how to look after itself
hints: A class body is `class Hero { public: ... private: ... };` - semicolon after the closing brace, exactly like a struct.
The constructor has the same name as the class and no return type: `Hero(std::string name, int maxHp) { ... }`. It runs when the object is made.
Trailing underscores (`hp_`, `name_`) are a common way to tell a member apart from a parameter with the same meaning. Nothing magic - just a habit that saves confusion.
`bool isAlive() const` - the `const` after the parentheses promises this method changes nothing. Put it on every method that only reads, and the compiler will catch you if you lie.
`status()` builds a string rather than printing one. Use `std::to_string(hp_)` to turn a number into text, and `+` to glue pieces together.

# FLOOR 14 - The Class of Heroes

Your `Monster` struct works, but nothing stops this:

```
goblin.hp = -9999;
```

The struct is a bag of variables and anyone can reach in. Every rule about
what a monster *is* - hp never below zero, never above max - lives scattered
in whatever functions happen to remember. Miss one and the game quietly
breaks.

A **class** fixes that by putting the data and the rules in the same box, and
then locking the box.

## The shape

```
class Hero {
public:
    Hero(std::string name, int maxHp) {
        name_ = name;
        maxHp_ = maxHp;
        hp_ = maxHp;
    }

    void takeDamage(int amount) {
        hp_ -= amount;
        if (hp_ < 0) { hp_ = 0; }
    }

    bool isAlive() const {
        return hp_ > 0;
    }

private:
    std::string name_;
    int hp_;
    int maxHp_;
};
```

- `public:` - what the outside world may use
- `private:` - what only the class itself may touch. This is the lock.
- the **constructor** shares the class's name, has no return type, and runs
  automatically when a Hero is made

`hp_` cannot be set to -9999 from outside, because there is no way in.
The only route is `takeDamage`, which has the rule built in. That is
**encapsulation**: the object protects its own promises.

## const methods

```
bool isAlive() const
```

That `const` after the parentheses is a promise: *this method does not
change the object*. The compiler enforces it - try to assign to `hp_`
inside a const method and it refuses to build. Put it on every method that
only reads. It is free, and it makes the class self-documenting.

## Using it

```
Hero h("Kaelen", 40);
h.takeDamage(12);
std::cout << h.status() << "\n";
```

The constructor arguments go right after the name. From then on it is just
dots, as with a struct - but now only the doors the class chose to open.

## Your task

Write a `Hero` class with private `name_`, `hp_` and `maxHp_`, and exactly
these public members:

```
Hero(std::string name, int maxHp)   // starts at full health
void takeDamage(int amount)         // never below 0
void heal(int amount)               // never above maxHp_
bool isAlive() const
std::string status() const          // "Kaelen 28/40"
```

`status` **returns** a string, it does not print one. Build it with
`std::to_string` and `+`.

In main, make `Hero kaelen("Kaelen", 40)` and produce exactly this:

```
Kaelen 40/40
takes 12 -> Kaelen 28/40
heals 30 -> Kaelen 40/40
takes 55 -> Kaelen 0/40
alive: no
heals 10 -> Kaelen 10/40
alive: yes
```

Notice `heals 30` only restores 12 of it, and `takes 55` stops at 0. The
main function never says so - the Hero enforces it, every time, without
being asked.

levels.title: The Locked Door
levels.tagline: const, and the promises a class keeps
hints: `Pack(size_t capacity)` only needs to store the capacity - the vector starts empty on its own.
`add` must check `full()` FIRST and return false without touching the vector. A method that half-succeeds is worse than one that refuses.
`drop` needs a hand-written search: walk the vector by index, and when `items_[i] == item`, erase it with `items_.erase(items_.begin() + i);` then `return true;` immediately.
`list()` returns a string. Join with `, ` BETWEEN items - the usual trick is `if (i > 0) out += ", ";` before appending item i.
`report` takes a `const Pack&`, so every method it calls must be const. If the compiler complains about that, you have found a method missing its const - that is the floor working as intended.
levels.brief:
# FLOOR 15 - The Locked Door

Floor 14 locked the data away. This floor is about the two things that make
that lock worth having: **invariants**, and **const**.

## An invariant is a promise

An invariant is something about your object that is true the moment it is
born and true after every method, no matter what anyone does to it.

- a Hero's hp is never below 0, never above maxHp
- a Pack never holds more than its capacity

Once a promise like that is enforced *inside* the class, every piece of code
outside can stop worrying about it. That is the actual payoff of
encapsulation - not secrecy, but the fact that there is exactly **one** place
that can break each rule, so there is exactly one place to look.

## Failure is a return value

What should `add` do when the pack is full? Not crash, and not silently
pretend. It should say so:

```
bool add(const std::string& item);   // false = did not fit
```

The caller decides what that means. Refuse cleanly and change nothing - a
method that half-succeeds is worse than one that says no.

## const, and why it spreads

```
void report(const Pack& p) {
    std::cout << p.size();     // only compiles if size() is const
}
```

`p` is a `const Pack&` - a promise that `report` will not change the pack.
So the compiler will only let it call methods that made the same promise.
One missing `const` on `size()` and this function will not build.

That is why const seems to spread through a codebase: it is not a style,
it is a chain of promises, and every link has to hold. Mark every
read-only method `const` and the chain builds itself.

## Your task

Write a `Pack` class:

```
Pack(size_t capacity)
bool add(const std::string& item)     // false if already full
bool drop(const std::string& item)    // false if it is not in there
bool has(const std::string& item) const
bool full() const
size_t size() const
size_t capacity() const
std::string list() const              // "torch, rope" or "(empty)"
```

Data: a `std::vector<std::string> items_` and a `size_t capacity_`, both
private.

Then a free function, outside the class:

```
void report(const Pack& p)
```

which prints two lines - `-- pack (<size>/<capacity>) --` and then
`p.list()`.

In main, make a `Pack pack(3);` and produce exactly this:

```
-- pack (0/3) --
(empty)
add torch -> yes
add rope -> yes
add rations -> yes
add lantern -> no
-- pack (3/3) --
torch, rope, rations
has rope: yes
drop rope -> yes
drop rope -> no
has rope: no
-- pack (2/3) --
torch, rations
```

The separator in `list()` is a comma followed by one space, and there is no
trailing comma. Getting that right is a five-minute fight the first time and
then a reflex forever.

# FLOOR 16 - Many Shapes of Monster   [BOSS]

You want a goblin, an ogre and a wraith in one list, and you want to write
the fight loop **once**. They are different types. A `std::vector<Goblin>`
cannot hold an ogre.

This is the problem inheritance exists to solve, and it is the last big idea
in the object half of C++.

## A Monster, and kinds of Monster

```
class Monster {
public:
    Monster(std::string name, int hp) : name_(name), hp_(hp) {}
    virtual ~Monster() = default;

    virtual std::string cry() const { return "..."; }
    virtual int attackRoll() const { return roll(4); }

    void takeDamage(int a) { hp_ -= a; if (hp_ < 0) hp_ = 0; }
    bool isAlive() const { return hp_ > 0; }
    const std::string& name() const { return name_; }
    int hp() const { return hp_; }

protected:
    std::string name_;
    int hp_;
};

class Goblin : public Monster {
public:
    Goblin() : Monster("goblin", 12) {}
    std::string cry() const override { return "yip!"; }
    int attackRoll() const override { return roll(4) + 1; }
};
```

Three new pieces of syntax:

- `: public Monster` - a Goblin **is a** Monster, and inherits everything.
- `: name_(name), hp_(hp)` after the constructor's parentheses is an
  **initialiser list**. It builds the members directly instead of default-building
  them and then assigning. `Goblin() : Monster("goblin", 12) {}` uses it to
  hand values up to the base class - which is the only way to do that.
- `protected:` - like private, except derived classes may also reach it.

## virtual and override

`virtual` says: a derived class is allowed to replace this. `override` says:
I am replacing something - and please check that I spelled it right. Without
`override`, a typo silently creates a brand new unrelated method and your
goblin quietly uses the base version forever. Always write it.

## Pointers, briefly

To keep different kinds in one vector, you store **addresses**:

```
std::vector<Monster*> horde;
horde.push_back(new Goblin());
```

- `Monster*` - "the address of some Monster"
- `new Goblin()` - build one that outlives this scope, hand back its address
- `m->cry()` - the dot, for pointers
- `delete m;` - hand the memory back

And here is the magic: `m` is a `Monster*`, but `m->cry()` runs **Goblin's**
version. The decision happens at run time, based on what the object really
is. One loop, three behaviours. That is **polymorphism**.

## The virtual destructor

```
virtual ~Monster() = default;
```

Deleting a Goblin through a `Monster*` when the destructor is not virtual is
undefined behaviour - the wrong destructor runs. Rule: **the moment a class
has one virtual function, give it a virtual destructor.**

Every `new` needs exactly one `delete`. Miss one and you have leaked memory.
Doing this by hand is tedious and error-prone, which is exactly why floor 20
exists.

## Your task

Build `Monster` as above, then three kinds:

| class  | name     | hp | cry         | attackRoll        |
|--------|----------|----|-------------|-------------------|
| Goblin | "goblin" | 12 | `yip!`      | `roll(4) + 1`     |
| Ogre   | "ogre"   | 30 | `GRAAA`     | `roll(6) + 3`     |
| Wraith | "wraith" | 8  | `(silence)` | *does not override* |

Wraith inherits the base `attackRoll` - do not give it one.

In main, put one of each into a `std::vector<Monster*>`, in that order, then:

1. print `-- the horde --`
2. for each: `<name>: <cry>`
3. print `-- they strike --`
4. for each: `<name> strikes for <attackRoll()>`
5. print `-- you answer --`
6. for each: 15 damage, then `<name> takes 15 (hp <left>)`, and if it died,
   a second line: two spaces, then `<name> is gone`
7. print `survivors: <count still alive>`
8. `delete` every one of them

Expected:

```
-- the horde --
goblin: yip!
ogre: GRAAA
wraith: (silence)
-- they strike --
goblin strikes for 5
ogre strikes for 6
wraith strikes for 2
-- you answer --
goblin takes 15 (hp 0)
  goblin is gone
ogre takes 15 (hp 15)
wraith takes 15 (hp 0)
  wraith is gone
survivors: 1
```

levels.brief:
# FLOOR 17 - The Save Stone

Everything your programs have ever done vanished the moment they exited.
A game needs to remember. Files are how.

The good news: you already know the syntax. A file stream is `cout` and
`cin` pointed somewhere else.

## Writing

```
#include <fstream>

std::ofstream out("save.txt");
out << "Kaelen\n";
out << 28 << " " << 40 << "\n";
```

`ofstream` is an **o**utput file stream. Opening it this way wipes the file
and starts fresh. You never close it - when `out` goes out of scope, it
closes itself. (Hold on to that. It is floor 20's whole subject.)

## Reading

```
std::ifstream in("save.txt");
int hp, maxHp;
in >> hp >> maxHp;
```

Same `>>`, same rules - including the newline trap from floor 13. If you
read numbers with `>>` and then want a whole line, clear the leftover first:

```
in >> count;
in.ignore(10000, '\n');
std::getline(in, item);
```

## Files that are not there

This is the part beginners skip and then spend an evening on. Opening a
missing file is **not** a crash. You get a stream that quietly fails, and
every read from it does nothing, leaving your variables holding garbage.

```
std::ifstream in("missing.txt");
if (!in) {
    std::cout << "no save file found\n";
}
```

Check every file you open. Always.

## Designing a format

A save file is a promise between the writer and the reader. Keep it dull and
obvious. Ours:

```
Kaelen          <- name, a whole line
28 40           <- hp and maxHp
137             <- gold
3               <- how many items follow
torch           <- the items, one per line
rope
iron key
```

The count line is the important idea: the reader must know how many items to
expect before it starts reading them.

## Your task

Three parts, in one program.

**Part 1** - write exactly the file above to `save.txt`, from these values:
name `Kaelen`, hp 28, maxHp 40, gold 137, and the three items `torch`,
`rope`, `iron key`. Then print:

```
saved to save.txt
```

**Part 2** - open `save.txt` fresh, read it all back into new variables, and
print:

```
-- loaded --
Kaelen 28/40
gold: 137
items: 3
  torch
  rope
  iron key
```

Read it back properly - do not print the variables you already had. The
point is the round trip.

**Part 3** - try to open `missing.txt`, check it, and print:

```
missing.txt: no save file found
```

The item lines in part 2 have two leading spaces. `iron key` has a space in
it, so those must come back with `getline`, not `>>`.

levels.brief:
# FLOOR 18 - The Bestiary

To find something in a vector you walk the whole thing. Twenty items, fine.
Twenty thousand, every frame, and your game is a slideshow.

When you want to look things up **by name**, you want a map.

## std::map

```
#include <map>

std::map<std::string, int> hoard;

hoard["rat"] = 3;
hoard["bat"] = 1;

std::cout << hoard["rat"];      // 3
std::cout << hoard.size();      // 2
```

Two type arguments: the **key** you look up by, and the **value** you get
back. Lookup does not scan - it goes more or less straight there.

A `std::map` also keeps its keys **sorted**. Print one and it comes out
alphabetically without you asking. (`std::unordered_map` is faster and does
not sort. Use that when you do not care about order.)

## Walking a map

Each entry is a pair:

```
for (const auto& entry : hoard) {
    std::cout << entry.first << " x" << entry.second << "\n";
}
```

`first` is the key, `second` is the value. Since C++17 you can unpack them
into real names, which is much easier to read:

```
for (const auto& [name, count] : hoard) {
    std::cout << name << " x" << count << "\n";
}
```

`auto` means "compiler, you work out the type". Here the type is a long
mouthful and `auto` is the normal choice.

## The trap: operator[] inserts

```
if (hoard["dragon"] > 0) { ... }
```

If `dragon` was not in the map, that line just **created** it, with value 0.
Your map grew a key by being asked a question. That is how a size count
slowly drifts wrong and nobody knows why.

To ask without inserting, use `find`:

```
auto it = hoard.find("dragon");
if (it == hoard.end()) {
    // not there
} else {
    std::cout << it->second;      // it is a pointer-ish thing, so ->
}
```

`end()` is "one past the last entry" - the universal C++ way of saying not
found.

Counting is the one place `hoard[name]++` is exactly right: you *want* a
missing key to spring into being as 0 and then become 1.

## Your task

Read item names, one per line, until `done`. Count how many times each one
appears, in a `std::map<std::string, int>`.

If nothing came in, print just this and stop:

```
the hoard is empty
```

Otherwise print:

```
-- hoard --
  <name> x<count>          (every entry, alphabetical - the map does this)
distinct: <how many different names>
total: <how many items altogether>
rat: <count, or "none">
gold coin: <count, or "none">
```

Those last two are **lookups done with `find`**, so that asking about
something absent does not add it. Print the number when it is there and the
word `none` when it is not.

For input `rat, bat, rat, gold coin, rat, bat, done`:

```
-- hoard --
  bat x2
  gold coin x1
  rat x3
distinct: 3
total: 6
rat: 3
gold coin: 1
```

Names can contain spaces, so read them with `getline`.

hints: `#include <memory>` for unique_ptr and make_unique, `#include <utility>` for std::move.
`horde.push_back(std::make_unique<Goblin>());` - make_unique builds it and hands the vector sole ownership. There is no `new` anywhere on this floor.

Loop with `for (const auto& m : horde)` when reading and `for (auto& m : horde)` when changing. A plain `auto m` would try to COPY a unique_ptr, which is forbidden on purpose - copying it would mean two owners.
`survivors.push_back(std::move(m));` hands ownership over. Afterwards `m` is empty - that is the point, there is only ever one owner.
`m.reset();` destroys what a unique_ptr holds, right now. On a pointer whose contents were already moved away it does nothing at all - which is exactly why the survivors do not dissolve in that loop.
Torch is pure RAII: a constructor that prints, a destructor that prints, nothing else. Declare it FIRST in main so it is destroyed LAST.
levels.brief:
# FLOOR 20 - The Weight of Memory   [BOSS]

Floor 16 ended with this:

```
for (Monster* m : horde) {
    delete m;
}
```

It works. It also has to be right *every single time*, including the times
you return early, and the times something throws halfway through. Miss one
and the memory is gone until the program exits. This is the single largest
source of serious bugs in C and C++.

Modern C++ mostly deleted the problem instead of solving it.

## RAII

The idea has a terrible name and is one of the best in the language:

> a thing that owns a resource releases it in its destructor

The destructor runs **automatically** when the object goes out of scope.
Not when you remember. Not on the happy path only. Always.

```
class Torch {
public:
    Torch(std::string where) : where_(where) {
        std::cout << "you light the torch in the " << where_ << "\n";
    }
    ~Torch() {
        std::cout << "the torch gutters out in the " << where_ << "\n";
    }
private:
    std::string where_;
};
```

`~Torch()` is the destructor - the class's name with a tilde. You have been
relying on this for floors: that is how every `std::string`, `std::vector`
and `std::ofstream` you have used cleaned itself up.

Objects are destroyed in **reverse** order of creation. First lit, last out.

## unique_ptr

Now apply RAII to the horde:

```
#include <memory>

std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Monster>> horde;
horde.push_back(std::make_unique<Goblin>());
```

A `unique_ptr` is a pointer that owns what it points at, and deletes it when
it dies. `make_unique<Goblin>()` builds a Goblin and hands over ownership.
No `new`, no `delete`, no leak - it is not possible to forget.

It still behaves like a pointer: `m->cry()` works exactly as before.

## Unique means unique

You cannot copy a `unique_ptr`. Two owners would both try to delete, so the
language refuses. To hand ownership over, you **move** it:

```
survivors.push_back(std::move(m));
```

After that line, `m` is empty and `survivors` owns the monster. Exactly one
owner, always. That is why your loops need `auto&` and not `auto` - a plain
`auto` would try to copy, and the compiler will stop you.

`m.reset()` destroys what a unique_ptr holds immediately. On one that has
already been moved from, it does nothing, because there is nothing left.

## Your task

Take floor 16's monsters, drop `attackRoll` (no dice today), and give the
base class a destructor that announces itself:

```
virtual ~Monster() { std::cout << "  " << name_ << " dissolves\n"; }
```

Keep `cry()` virtual: goblin `yip!`, ogre `GRAAA`, wraith `(silence)`.
Keep hp: goblin 12, ogre 30, wraith 8. Write the `Torch` class as above.

In main, in this order:

1. `Torch torch("hall");` - first, so it dies last
2. a `std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Monster>> horde` with a Goblin, an Ogre and
   a Wraith, made with `make_unique`
3. print `-- the horde --`, then `<name>: <cry>` for each
4. print `-- you answer --`, then hit each for 15: `<name> takes 15 (hp <left>)`
5. print `-- the dead are cleared --`, then move every *living* monster into a
   second vector `survivors`, and afterwards `reset()` each pointer in `horde`
   in order
6. print `survivors: <count>`
7. print `-- you leave --`

Then just let main end. Write no `delete` at all.

```
you light the torch in the hall
-- the horde --
goblin: yip!
ogre: GRAAA
wraith: (silence)
-- you answer --
goblin takes 15 (hp 0)
ogre takes 15 (hp 15)
wraith takes 15 (hp 0)
-- the dead are cleared --
  goblin dissolves
  wraith dissolves
survivors: 1
-- you leave --
  ogre dissolves
the torch gutters out in the hall
```

Look at the last three lines. Nothing in your code printed them at that
point. The ogre dissolves because `survivors` went out of scope, and the
torch goes out after it because it was made first. You wrote no cleanup and
nothing leaked.

That is the floor. Everything above this one is now yours to build with.

# FLOOR 21 - The Dungeon Map

Five floors left, and they are all the same project. By floor 25 you will
have a real, playable game - a dungeon you walk through, with monsters that
fight back, loot, a locked door and a save file. You are going to write it.

Everything you need, you already know. The only new thing is *scale*: from
here on you are building a program with parts, not a program with a task.

## A world is a grid of characters

```
####################
#@...#........#....#
#....#..####..#..!.#
```

`#` rock, `.` floor, `@` you, `!` a potion, `$` gold, `k` a key, `>` the
way down. That is the entire graphics engine, and games shipped like this
for twenty years.

In code it is a `std::vector<std::string>`. Each string is one row:

```
rows_[y][x]
```

**y first.** `rows_[y]` picks the row, `[x]` picks the character in it.
Everyone gets this backwards at least once - usually by writing `rows_[x][y]`
and then staring at a dungeon that is somehow inside out.

## Out of bounds is not an error, it is a decision

`rows_[99][99]` on a 20x12 map is undefined behaviour: no crash, no warning,
just garbage or a corruption you find three hours later.

So the map never gets asked directly. Everything goes through:

```
char Dungeon::tileAt(int x, int y) const {
    if (x < 0 || y < 0 || x >= width() || y >= height()) {
        return '#';
    }
    return rows_[y][x];
}
```

Outside the map is solid rock. Now movement code, monster code and rendering
code can ask about any coordinate at all and get a sensible answer. One
guard, written once, and a whole category of bug is gone.

That habit - **make the invalid case impossible to reach rather than
remembering to avoid it** - is most of what separates code that works from
code that works today.

## The player is not on the map

The map stores terrain. Where the hero is standing is a *different* fact,
and it lives in different variables. `render` takes the player position and
draws `@` on top:

```
if (x == playerX && y == playerY) std::cout << '@';
else                              std::cout << rows_[y][x];
```

If you wrote the `@` into `rows_` instead, moving would mean erasing the old
one and remembering what used to be underneath. Try it once, some day, to
feel why nobody does it.

## Your task

`dungeon.h` and `main.cpp` are written for you. Read `dungeon.h` first - it
is the contract. Then write `dungeon.cpp`.

The constructor builds `rows_` from the map below, finds the `@`, records it
in `startX_` / `startY_`, and replaces that tile with `.`:

```
####################
#@...#........#....#
#....#..####..#..!.#
#....#..#..#..#....#
#.####..#..#..####.#
#....#..#..#.......#
#.$..#..#.##..####.#
#....#........#..#.#
#.####.########..#.#
#......#k........#.#
#.####............>#
####################
```

Then implement `width`, `height`, `tileAt`, `setTile`, `isWall`, `render`,
`startX` and `startY` - all of them out of line, with `Dungeon::`.

`isWall` is `tileAt(x, y) == '#'`. `setTile` must ignore out-of-range
coordinates rather than crash.

Running `main.cpp` should give you:

```
-- THE DUNGEON OF THE NULL POINTER --
size: 20x12
start: 1,1
```

followed by the map with `@` at 1,1, some tile queries, and the map again
with `@` standing on the gold at 2,6.

> Every `.cpp` in your workspace gets compiled and linked together, exactly
> like floor 19. You will be adding more files each floor from here.

# FLOOR 22 - First Steps

The dungeon exists. Nobody is in it yet.

This floor adds the thing that makes software a *game*: a loop that reads
what the player wants, changes the world, and shows them the result. Read,
update, draw. Every game ever written is that loop.

## The shape

```
while (std::getline(std::cin, cmd)) {
    // 1. work out what they meant
    // 2. change the world
    // 3. show them
}
```

Your `while (level < 5)` from floor 5 waited for a number to change. This one
waits for a person. When `getline` finally returns false the input has run
out - which for you now means the player closed the game.

## Where the player is

The hero is not on the map (floor 21). Their position is two ints in `main`:

```
int px = d.startX();
int py = d.startY();
```

## Try, then commit

The wrong way to move:

```
py = py - 1;
if (d.isWall(px, py)) { py = py + 1; }   // oops, put it back
```

That works until something else runs between the two lines, and then you have
a hero standing inside a wall. The right way is to look before you leap:

```
int nx = px;
int ny = py;
if (cmd == "w") { ny = py - 1; }
...
if (d.isWall(nx, ny)) {
    std::cout << "a wall blocks you\n";
} else {
    px = nx;
    py = ny;
    ...
}
```

Compute the target, test the target, *then* commit. The player is never in an
invalid state, not even for one line.

**Up is minus one.** Row 0 is the top of the map, so `w` decreases `y`. This
feels wrong for about a week and then never again.

## Your task

`dungeon.h` and `dungeon.cpp` are already in your workspace - the reference
version from floor 21, so every floor from here starts from the same ground.
You write `main.cpp`.

Start by printing:

```
-- THE DUNGEON OF THE NULL POINTER --
w a s d to move, q to leave
```

then render the map with the hero at the start position.

Then loop over lines of input:

- `w` `a` `s` `d` - try to move north, west, south, east
  - if the target is a wall: print `a wall blocks you` and nothing else
  - otherwise: move, print `you step <north|west|south|east>`, then render
- `q` - print `you climb back out.` and leave the loop
- anything else - print `you cannot do that.`

When the loop ends for any reason - `q` or the input running out - print:

```
steps taken: <n>
```

Only successful moves count as steps. Bumping a wall is not a step.

If the input runs out without a `q`, print `the dungeon goes quiet.` before
the steps line.

The start of a run with input `d`, `d`, `w`, `s`, `s`, `q`:

```
-- THE DUNGEON OF THE NULL POINTER --
w a s d to move, q to leave
####################
#@...#........#....#
...
you step east
####################
#.@..#........#....#
...
```

> Play it yourself with `.\play.ps1 run` before you check it. Walk into a few
> walls. This is the first thing you have written that is genuinely fun to
> poke at, and poking at it is how you will find the bugs.

# FLOOR 23 - Things That Fight Back

Your `main` is about to get too big. That is not a style complaint - it is a
structural one. It holds the map, the player position, the step count and the
loop, and every new feature adds another loose variable that some other part
of the code has to be trusted not to break.

Floor 14 already gave you the answer: put the data and the rules in the same
box.

## The Game class

```
class Game {
public:
    Game();
    void run();

private:
    void draw() const;
    void step(int dx, int dy);
    void monstersAct();
    Monster* monsterAt(int x, int y);

    Dungeon dungeon_;
    std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Monster>> monsters_;
    int px_, py_, hp_, maxHp_, steps_;
    bool running_;
};
```

Now `main.cpp` is four lines, and every part of the game can see the state it
needs without any of it being global. A Game **has a** Dungeon and **has**
Monsters - that is **composition**, and it is the relationship you will reach
for far more often than inheritance.

## Owning versus borrowing

The game owns the monsters:

```
std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Monster>> monsters_;
```

But `monsterAt` only wants to *point at* one:

```
Monster* Game::monsterAt(int x, int y) {
    for (auto& m : monsters_) {
        if (m->isAlive() && m->x() == x && m->y() == y) {
            return m.get();
        }
    }
    return nullptr;
}
```

`m.get()` hands out the raw address **without** giving away ownership. The
caller may look and poke; the vector still owns it and will still clean it up.
That split - one owner, many borrowers - is how modern C++ is written.

`nullptr` is the answer to "there is nothing here". Check it before you use
it, every time:

```
Monster* target = monsterAt(nx, ny);
if (target != nullptr) { ... }
```

Dereferencing a null pointer is how this dungeon got its name.

## Bump to attack

The classic roguelike control scheme: walking into a monster is attacking it.
One key, two meanings, decided by what is there.

```
if (target != nullptr)      attack it, and do not move
else if (isWall(nx, ny))    blocked
else                        move
```

## Your task

`dice.*` and `dungeon.*` are done. `monster.h`, `game.h` and `main.cpp` are
written for you - read all three before you start. You write `monster.cpp`
and `game.cpp`.

> Every capstone floor hands you the reference version of the previous floor,
> so a wobble on floor 22 cannot sink floor 25. Your own floor 22 `main.cpp`
> is still in its own workspace folder if you want it.

**monster.cpp** - the constructor, the getters, `takeDamage` (never below 0),
`isAlive`, the base `cry()` returning `...` and base `damageRoll()` returning
`roll(attack_)`, then:

| class  | name     | glyph | hp | attack | cry     | damageRoll     |
|--------|----------|-------|----|--------|---------|----------------|
| Goblin | "goblin" | `g`   | 12 | 3      | `yip!`  | *inherited*    |
| Ogre   | "ogre"   | `O`   | 30 | 6      | `GRAAA` | `roll(6) + 3`  |

**game.cpp** - the constructor places the hero at the dungeon start with 30 hp
and creates three monsters, in this order:

```
Goblin at 4,5
Goblin at 9,9
Ogre   at 14,10
```

`draw()` prints the map with living monsters drawn over the terrain and the
hero over everything, then a status line:

```
hp 30/30   steps 0   monsters alive 3
```

`run()` prints the two header lines, draws once, then loops over input:

- `q` -> `you climb back out.` and stop
- `w` `a` `s` `d` -> `step(0,-1)`, `step(-1,0)`, `step(0,1)`, `step(1,0)`
- anything else -> `you cannot do that.` and nothing else happens

`step(dx, dy)`:

- a living monster on the target square -> you attack it for `roll(6) + 2`:
  `you hit the goblin for 7 (goblin hp 5)`, and if it died, `the goblin dies`.
  You do **not** move.
- otherwise a wall -> `a wall blocks you`, and the turn does not happen at all
- otherwise -> move, count a step, `you step east`

After a move or an attack (but not after a blocked bump, and not after
nonsense), `monstersAct()` runs: every living monster orthogonally adjacent to
the hero hits for its `damageRoll()`:

```
the goblin hits you for 3 (hp 27)
```

If that takes the hero to 0, print `you die in the dark.` and stop the game
immediately - no more drawing.

Then `draw()`.

At the end, whatever happened, print `steps taken: <n>`.

> Play it before you check it. Go and find the ogre at the bottom right - it
> hits for `roll(6) + 3` and you have 30 hp, so that fight is a real decision.

# FLOOR 24 - What the Dungeon Keeps

Walking and stabbing. Time for the third verb: **taking**.

This floor is mostly about reuse. The `Pack` you wrote on floor 15 - capacity,
add, drop, has, list - is exactly the pack this game needs. Go and get it.
That is not cheating, that is what writing a class was *for*.

## The world is allowed to change

Until now the dungeon has been read-only. Now the hero picks up a coin and
the coin has to stop being there:

```
dungeon_.setTile(px_, py_, '.');
```

That one line is the difference between an item and an infinite item. You
wrote `setTile` on floor 21 and have not used it once. This is why it exists.

Pickups happen **after** the move commits, when `px_` and `py_` are already
the new square. Look at what you are standing on, react, then erase it.

## Turns are a currency

Not every command costs a turn, and deciding which do is game design, not
programming:

- checking your inventory: free. Nobody gets hit for looking in a bag.
- drinking a potion: **a turn**. Monsters get to act. That is the whole
  tension - heal now and take a hit, or run and hope.
- trying to drink a potion you do not have: free. You did nothing.

In code that is just where you put `continue`. A tiny decision that changes
how the game feels to play.

## Your task

Your workspace arrives holding the reference floor 23 game, so a wobble back
there cannot sink this floor.

`pack.h` is given. Write `pack.cpp` - the floor 15 methods, out of line, with
`Pack::` on the front. Then extend `game.cpp`.

**The Game gains** `int gold_ = 0;` and `Pack pack_{6};` (both already
declared in the new `game.h`).

**The status line** grows a field:

```
hp 30/30   gold 0   steps 0   monsters alive 3
```

**After a successful move**, look at the tile you landed on:

- `$` -> `gold_ += roll(20) + 10;` then `you scoop up <n> gold` and clear the tile
- `!` -> try `pack_.add("potion")`.
  - it fitted -> `you pocket a potion.` and clear the tile
  - it did not -> `your pack is full.` and **leave the potion where it is**
- `k` -> `pack_.add("iron key")`, `you pocket the iron key.`, clear the tile
- anything else -> nothing

Do this before the monsters act.

**Two new commands:**

`i` - free, no turn:

```
-- pack (1/6) --
potion
gold: 137
```

(the second line is `pack_.list()`)

`p` - drink a potion:

- no potion -> `you have no potions.`, free, no turn
- otherwise -> drop one, heal `roll(8) + 8` capped at `maxHp_`, print
  `you drink a potion (hp 30/30)`, and this **is** a turn: monsters act,
  then draw.

The second header line now advertises them:

```
w a s d to move, i for your pack, p to drink, q to leave
```

Everything else from floor 23 stays exactly as it was.

> With gold on the map and a pack that fills up, this is now a game with
> decisions in it. Go and play it properly - walk to the gold at the bottom
> left, then across to the potion in the top right, and see whether the
> ogre lets you reach the key.

levels.brief:
# FLOOR 25 - The Last Door   [FINAL]

One floor left. Your game can be walked through, fought in and looted. It
cannot be **won**, and it cannot be **left and come back to**. Both of those
are what turns a toy into a game, and you have already learned everything
they need.

## An ending is just a state

A game without a win condition is a screensaver with opinions. Yours has a
door at the bottom right and a key hidden behind a goblin. That is a whole
game design: a goal, an obstacle, and a reason to go the long way round.

```
if (dungeon_.tileAt(px_, py_) != '>') return;

if (pack_.has("iron key")) {
    // won
} else {
    // locked
}
```

Notice the ogre standing between you and that door. Nothing in the code says
"the ogre guards the exit" - it emerges from a position and a damage roll.
That is level design, and you just did some.

## Saving is writing your state down

A save file is every piece of mutable state, in an order the reader agrees
with. Look at what your Game actually holds:

- where the hero is, their hp, gold and step count
- the terrain, because loot has been taken off it
- each monster's remaining hp
- what is in the pack

Anything you leave out comes back wrong. Anything you write in a different
order than you read comes back scrambled. That is the whole craft of it.

`tileAt` and `setTile` are exact inverses, which is what makes the map
round-trip cleanly. Small interfaces pay you back later.

And once more, for the third and last time: after reading a number with
`>>`, clear the leftover newline before you `getline`.

## Your task

Your workspace arrives holding the reference floor 24 game, plus updated
`monster.h`, `pack.h` and `game.h`. Three small additions and one big one.

**monster.cpp** - implement `void Monster::setHp(int hp)`. A loaded game has
wounded monsters.

**pack.cpp** - implement `const std::vector<std::string>& Pack::items() const`,
returning `items_`. The save needs to walk them one by one, which `list()`
cannot do.

**game.cpp:**

`void Game::checkExit()` - called from `step()` right after `pickUp()`.

- not standing on `>` -> nothing happens
- on `>` without the key -> `the door is iron, and locked. something in here opens it.`
- on `>` with the key -> the hero wins:

```
=====================================
  YOU CLIMB THE STAIR INTO DAYLIGHT
=====================================
gold: 137
steps: 42
monsters slain: 1
```

then `running_ = false;` and `won_ = true;` - no monsters act, no map is drawn.

`void Game::save()` - write `dungeon.sav`, in exactly this order:

```
<px> <py>
<hp> <maxHp>
<gold> <steps>
<width> <height>
<height lines of raw terrain, from tileAt>
<how many monsters>
<one line per monster: its hp>
<how many items in the pack>
<one line per item>
```

then print `saved.`

`void Game::load()` - read it back in the same order and print `loaded.`,
then `draw()`. If the file is not there, print `no save file found.` and
change nothing. Empty the pack with `pack_ = Pack(6);` before refilling it,
or loading twice gives you two of everything.

`void Game::help() const` - print:

```
-- commands --
w a s d   move, or attack whatever you walk into
i         look in your pack
p         drink a potion
save      write dungeon.sav
load      read dungeon.sav
?         this list
q         give up
```

**Wire them into run().** `save`, `load`, `i` and `?` are all **free** - they
cost no turn and no monster acts. Update the header line to:

```
w a s d to move, i pack, p potion, ? help, q leave
```

`steps taken: <n>` still prints at the very end, after everything, win or
lose.

## And then you are done

When the trials pass, `workspace\25-the-last-door` holds roughly seven hundred
lines of C++ across eleven files: a dungeon, a monster hierarchy, an
inventory, a combat system, a save format and a game loop. You wrote it.

Play it properly before you check it. Find the key. Get past the ogre. Save
before you try something stupid.

Then open a new folder and build the next one - a bigger map, a shop, a
second dungeon level, monsters that chase you. Nothing in this tower is
holding you up any more.
